source: T-6A Techniques and Procedures Manual (I.N. T-6A 02/14, Change 9 Jul 22)

sections.title: INTRODUCTION (Section 8A—General)
sections.technique_summary: Navigation training covers techniques and procedures used to fly from one location to another. The chapter also covers use of unfamiliar airfields, decision making outside the local area, task management, cockpit organization (complicated by charts and additional FLIP pubs), and VFR mission planning. Instruction Notes «3-6/12 (pages 100-122)» is the primary source for information on navigation.

parameters.name: primary reference for navigation
parameters.verbatim: Instruction Notes «3-6/12 (pages 100-122)» is the primary source for information on navigation.

sections.title: GENERAL
sections.technique_summary: Mission preparation may begin several days before departure. Destinations and routes may be selected anytime in the planning process; however, some flight planning tasks, such as wind computations, fuel calculations, and weather briefings, must be completed shortly before departure. IFR and VFR refer to rules and procedures while IMC and VMC refer to conditions. Conditions must generally be VMC to fly using VFR, but conditions can be either IMC or VMC to fly using IFR.
procedure_steps: Begin mission preparation several days before departure where possible.
Select destinations and routes at any point in the planning process.
Complete wind computations, fuel calculations and weather briefings shortly before departure.
common_errors: Confusing instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) / visual meteorological conditions (VMC) with instrument flight rules (IFR) / visual flight rules (VFR) — IFR and VFR refer to rules and procedures while IMC and VMC refer to conditions.
sections.notes: The general guidelines of Section 8A apply to the planning and execution of any type of navigation mission (for example IFR, VFR, or VFR low-level).

sections.title: MISSION PLANNING (General)
sections.technique_summary: Basic considerations to determine if an airfield is acceptable for use include runway length, servicing capability, command restrictions, operating hours, and instrument approach availability. Strange fields are fields that the pilot is unfamiliar with, and require additional planning effort. NOTAMs, actual and forecast weather, flight plan filing, TOLD computation and unit navigation checklists complete the planning cycle. A common memory aid to ensure completion of major planning steps is WANTS.

parameters.name: flight plan A/C type
parameters.verbatim: Use “TEX2” as type of A/C.

parameters.name: flight plan reference
parameters.value: FLIP General Planning, Chapter 4, or M.A.I.P GREECE (VOL-3)
parameters.verbatim: Consult FLIP General Planning, Chapter 4, or M.A.I.P GREECE (VOL-3), for guidelines on completion of the Flight Plan Form.

procedure_steps: 8.3.1 Choosing a Destination — assess runway length, servicing capability, command restrictions, operating hours, and instrument approach availability.
8.3.2 NOTAM — perform an initial scan of the NOTAMs and a flight path search on the NOTAMs homepage to identify possible emergency airfields that may not be used due to runway closure.
8.3.3 Weather — study long-range forecasts several days in advance; check weather and winds for emergency fields along the route.
8.3.4 Flight Plan — complete and file the Flight Plan Form at Base Ops or via telephone; use “TEX2” as type of A/C.
8.3.5 TOLD — compute TOLD with the abbreviated checklist when off-station.

8.3.6 Navigation Checklists — use the WANTS memory aid: W - Weather (enroute, destination, minima); A - Activate flight plan (complete and file); N - NOTAMS (check for destination and drop-in airfields); T - TOLD (compute); S - SID (review departure procedure).
common_errors: Excessive distance (time and/or fuel required) can preclude completion of required approach training.
Weather conditions may not allow completion of major training objectives (for example, VFR low-level) or use of an otherwise excellent airfield (weather below minimums).
Failing to scan NOTAMs early, so that issues which eliminate potential destinations are found only after wasted planning effort.
Planning to a strange field without allowing the additional planning effort such fields require.
corrections: An initial scan of the NOTAMs can identify issues that eliminate potential destinations from planning consideration and prevent wasted effort.
Performing a flight path search on the NOTAMs homepage will identify possible emergency airfields that may not be used due to runway closure.

sections.title: RADIO PROCEDURES
sections.technique_summary: Standard radio calls, used at home station, simplify communications, and reduce radio congestion in the highly regulated local flying environment.
procedure_steps: Use standard radio calls as used at home station.

sections.title: TASK MANAGEMENT AND / OR COCKPIT ORGANIZATION
sections.technique_summary: The principles for instrument sorties also apply to navigation sorties (see paragraph 7.5.1); however, navigation sorties may be more complex and require more organization. For example, a navigation sortie could include an IFR portion to a VFR low-level followed by VFR point-to-point navigation to the destination and concluded with practice instrument approaches. In general, strive to find ways to get ahead and prepare for upcoming tasks.
procedure_steps: Apply the instrument-sortie cockpit organization principles of paragraph 7.5.1.
Add organization proportional to the added complexity of the navigation sortie.
Strive to find ways to get ahead and prepare for upcoming tasks.
common_errors: Treating a navigation sortie with the same level of organization as a local instrument sortie, although navigation sorties may be more complex and require more organization.

sections.title: GROUND OPERATIONS (General / off-station)
sections.technique_summary: At strange fields, use caution for other transient A/C and use the airfield diagram during taxi. Some civilian fields are not accustomed to operations with military A/C; it is the pilot's responsibility to ensure the safety of civilian ground personnel. After engine shutdown, complete the Before Leaving A/C Checklist and conduct a thorough post flight inspection. The aircrew is ultimately responsible for the A/C when off-station.

parameters.name: sunshade temperature threshold
parameters.verbatim: When planning for destination where the temperature may exceed 35° C carry sunshades. Install the sunshades when the temperatures exceed 35° C and the canopy must be closed.

parameters.name: minimum chocking
parameters.verbatim: Before departing the A/C ensure, at a minimum, the nose wheel is chocked.

parameters.name: strong wind chocking
parameters.verbatim: If strong winds are in the forecast, triple chock the A/C.

parameters.name: mooring guidance
parameters.value: wing and tail points, plus nose gear in windy/extreme conditions
parameters.verbatim: «wing and tail points provide sufficient mooring in normal conditions. However, when windy or extreme conditions are anticipated, the nose gear should also be secured».

procedure_steps: Use caution for other transient A/C at strange fields and use the airfield diagram during taxi.
After engine shutdown, complete the Before Leaving A/C Checklist and conduct a thorough post flight inspection of the A/C.
Ensure transient maintenance personnel are thoroughly familiar with all servicing requirements per the flight crew checklist, strange-field procedures section.
Stay with the A/C until refuelling is complete and ensure the A/C is properly secured.
Provide transient maintenance or Building Of Communication (BOC) personnel with contact information.
Before leaving base operations or the FBO, check the overnight and next day's weather.
If thunderstorms are forecast, attempt to hanger the A/C.
Always have a ground observer and fire bottle available for engine starts.
common_errors: Leaving the A/C unchocked: the parking brake system will bleed over time and with strong winds at night, a pilot may find their T-6 has moved, if not chocked.

Assuming transient servicing capability will be adequate — even after careful preflight planning, unforeseen circumstances may result in degraded transient servicing capability, such as absence of proper servicing fluids and/or equipment.
Overlooking that some civilian fields are not accustomed to operations with military A/C.
corrections: If any doubt exists as to transient maintenance's ability to properly and safely service the A/C, contact the home station before servicing the A/C.
Tie down ropes may also be used to anchor the A/C down.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION (Section 8B—IFR Navigation)
sections.technique_summary: Missions conducted under IFR rely on NAVAIDs and A/C instrumentation for navigation, situational awareness, and A/C control. The enroute IFR structure is very different from the local pattern.

sections.title: MISSION PLANNING (IFR)
sections.technique_summary: The general considerations of paragraph 8.3 apply. A leg length of approximately 300 miles allows for multiple approaches at the destination. If IMC conditions are anticipated, give special attention to the weather brief and review weather minima to determine takeoff and landing minimums.

parameters.name: IFR leg length
parameters.verbatim: A leg length of approximately 300 miles allows for multiple approaches at the destination.

procedure_steps: Choose a destination using the general considerations; target a leg length of approximately 300 miles.
Review weather minima to determine takeoff and landing minimums when IMC is anticipated.
common_errors: Failing to use caution for enroute hazards, such as embedded thunderstorms, icing, and turbulence, if IMC anticipated enroute.

sections.title: ROUTE PLANNING (IFR) / IFR NAVIGATION MISSION CARD
sections.technique_summary: Training sorties are typically flown on airways; GPS routing may also be used. Cruising altitude is determined from leg length. The IFR Navigation Mission Card is an approved flight log; use of all columns can help ensure accurate time and fuel planning. Exact methodology for use of the IFR Navigation Mission Card is technique.

parameters.name: cruise altitude rule of thumb
parameters.verbatim: One technique is to use 10 % of the distance for cruise altitude (for example, cruise at 15.000 feet MSL on a 150 NM leg).

parameters.name: start, taxi and takeoff (STTO) fuel
parameters.verbatim: As a starting point, use 50 pounds for start, taxi, and takeoff (STTO).

parameters.name: double-entry climb calculation threshold
parameters.verbatim: Use a double-entry climb calculation if field elevation is more than 5000 feet.

parameters.name: level-off distance
parameters.value: equals level-off altitude, up to FL250
parameters.verbatim: Level-off distance equals level-off altitude (up to FL250).

parameters.name: initial penetration and approach allowance
parameters.verbatim: Use approximately 15 minutes and 100 pounds for initial penetration and approach.

parameters.name: subsequent approach allowance
parameters.verbatim: Use approximately 50 pounds and 10 minutes for subsequent approaches if being vectored to final.

parameters.name: average TAS effect on climb
parameters.verbatim: Average TAS has a negligible effect on climb calculations.

parameters.name: Figure 8.1 example card — squawk
parameters.verbatim: SQUAWK__3256___

parameters.name: Figure 8.1 example card — rotation / abort speed
parameters.verbatim: ROTATION SPEED : 85 ABORT SPEED: 85

parameters.name: Figure 8.1 example card — remaining RWY length
parameters.verbatim: REMAINING RWY LENGTH: 7000 FT

parameters.name: Figure 8.1 example card — totals
parameters.value: TOTAL DIST 95, TOTAL ETE 0+41, TOTAL FUEL 2 + 03
parameters.verbatim: TOTALDIST95TOTAL ETE0+41TOTALFUEL2 + 03

procedure_steps: Plan the route on airways (GPS routing may also be used).
Determine cruising altitude based on leg length (technique: 10 % of the distance).
Use computerized tools (PFPS/Falcon View, etc.) when authorized, and check the results for reasonability before flight.
Fill all columns of the IFR Navigation Mission Card.
Track frequencies, NAVAIDs, and clearances in appropriate blocks.
common_errors: Accepting computerized planning output without a reasonability check — bad input can lead to bad output.
Leaving columns of the IFR Navigation Mission Card unused, degrading time and fuel planning accuracy.
sections.notes: Figure 8.1 shows a typical IFR leg from KALAMATA AFB to ARA.

sections.title: GROUND OPS (IFR)
sections.technique_summary: IFR clearance is generally received on CH-4 (Approach frequency) or on a clearance delivery frequency (found on the approach plate). The clearance should mirror what was filed on the Flight Plan Form; however, clearances may be changed by ATC. One technique to copy down and organize a clearance is to write down CHADS, then fill in the appropriate information after each letter. Review the airfield diagram before taxi request.

parameters.name: clearance frequency
parameters.value: CH-4 (Approach frequency) or clearance delivery frequency
parameters.verbatim: IFR clearance is generally received on CH-4 (Approach frequency) or on a clearance delivery frequency (found on the approach plate).

parameters.name: CHADS example — Altitude
parameters.verbatim: A - Altitude: A – 10.

parameters.name: CHADS example — Departure frequency
parameters.verbatim: D - Departure frequency: D - 120.75

parameters.name: CHADS example — Squawk
parameters.verbatim: S - Squawk: S – 3456.

parameters.name: radio call example — squawk / level
parameters.verbatim: «You are cleared from LGKL to LGKL via A14-ARA-H51-KESAL-PRV-DCT-ARA-DCT KAM,( or via flight planed route), squawk 7523, FL 180».

procedure_steps: Request ATC clearance, e.g. «Kalamata Approach Mistras 14 on Ground, ATC clearance».
Copy and organize the clearance using CHADS: C - Clearance (e.g. AF, As Filed); H - Heading (e.g. RWY); A - Altitude; D - Departure frequency; S - Squawk.
Review the airfield diagram before taxi request.
Request progressive taxi instructions if necessary.
common_errors: Expecting the clearance always to mirror what was filed — clearances may be changed by ATC (routing, heading after take-off, altitude, departure frequency, squawk, etc.).
corrections: Request progressive taxi instructions if necessary (to receive specific directions on where to turn and when from parking spot to the takeoff runway).

sections.title: DEPARTURE (IFR)
sections.technique_summary: Review departure routing and altitude restrictions before takeoff. Set NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff. The departure routing and altitudes may change just before takeoff or while on departure. An approach plate for the departure airfield should be readily available and reviewed for critical details in case of emergency return. Solid planning increases flexibility and ability to maintain situational awareness in the face of changes to the original plan.
procedure_steps: Review the approach plate to determine take-off restrictions, for example, departure procedure (Trouble T), SID, etc.
Plan to use preferred routings if applicable, to avoid significant route changes when issued clearance.
Review departure routing and altitude restrictions before takeoff.
Set NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff.
Keep an approach plate for the departure airfield readily available for emergency return.
common_errors: Not planning preferred routings, leading to significant route changes when issued clearance.
Being unprepared for departure routing and altitude changes that may occur just before takeoff or while on departure.
sections.notes: Paragraph 8.9.7 also directs reviewing planned approaches during pre-flight planning, and 8.9.8 to choose an alternate if required using the same factors as when choosing a primary location.

sections.title: ENROUTE (IFR)
sections.technique_summary: At level off, keep climb power until approaching the planned IAS, then set the planned fuel flow to hold the IAS. Adjust the PCL as needed to maintain the mission planned IAS. Accomplish a ground speed check to determine the effects of winds and use the actual fuel flow on the EID to calculate fuels. Maintain positional awareness at all times with NAVAIDs, GPS, VFR chart, and enroute chart, and periodically identify suitable emergency airfields.

parameters.name: enroute descent gradient technique
parameters.verbatim: One technique is to plan a 5° descent gradient for a 2:1 ratio between distance (NM to descend) and altitude (in thousands of feet) and then add an extra 10 miles for an instrument approach.

parameters.name: descent request example
parameters.verbatim: For example: For a descent from FL 200, request a descent approximately 50 miles out (2 multiplied by 20 plus 10 = 50 NM).

parameters.name: groundspeed by timing
parameters.value: DME change over one minute = groundspeed in miles per minute
parameters.verbatim: Simply note the DME change over one minute to determine groundspeed in miles per minute.

procedure_steps: At level off, keep climb power until approaching the planned IAS, then set the planned fuel flow to hold the IAS.
Adjust the PCL as needed to maintain the mission planned IAS.

Accomplish a ground speed check to determine the effects of winds (GPS is the easiest, most convenient way; groundspeed can also be read off the EHSI if selected when flying directly to or from a NAVAID; alternatively, timing can be used if altitude is greater than the range from the station).
Use groundspeed and fuel flow to predict fuel at future points on the route; compare planned, updated, and actual fuel at these points.
Maintain positional awareness at all times with NAVAIDs, GPS, VFR chart, and enroute chart.
Periodically identify suitable emergency airfields and practice decision making with what if drills (use of the GPS nearest function can be a valuable tool).
If an enroute descent is planned, determine the desired start-down point and attempt to get ATC clearance that matches the desired descent profile.
Prepare for arrival in accordance with AFMAN 11-217, Volume 1.
common_errors: Poor task prioritization during the busiest portions of off-station sorties — from the clearance call to level-off and from descent to engine shutdown — where the majority of safety incidents occur.
Without the cues associated with the local training environment, it is easy to forget required in-flight checks.
Failing to notice that modifications to the planned routing, altitude, winds, temperature, or excessive delays can drastically change the actual fuels from the planned fuels.
corrections: Stay busy and use memory aids, as necessary, to comply with all requirements.
Significant deviations between planned and actual fuel may require changes to the flight plan.
If ATC requires a descent earlier or later than desired, adjust the descent gradient using techniques described in Chapter 7.

sections.title: ARRIVAL (IFR)
sections.technique_summary: Navigation sorties typically terminate at other than the home field. Arrival at a strange field (neither pilot familiar) takes additional planning effort. From prior review, the pilot should be familiar with airfield layout, approach lighting, type of glide path guidance, field elevation, runway data, tower and ground control frequencies, etc. However, airfield information must be reviewed before arrival and landing. Match the planned arrival to the training objectives for the sortie.
procedure_steps: Consult AFMAN 11-217, Volume 1, and Chapter 7 for detailed information about IFR arrival.
Review airfield layout, approach lighting, glide path guidance type, field elevation, runway data, and tower/ground frequencies before arrival and landing.
Match the planned arrival to the training objectives for the sortie.
Coordinate requests for additional approaches as early as possible with ATC (approach control) and be flexible.
common_errors: Selecting approach procedures that require extensive cruise at lower altitudes, which may not be desirable because of excessive fuel consumption.
Relying on prior familiarity instead of reviewing airfield information before arrival and landing.
sections.notes: Pre-arrival tasks are the same as for instrument sorties. Figure 8.2 shows a typical IFR Navigation Flight.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION (Section 8C—VFR Navigation)
sections.technique_summary: VFR navigation can be more demanding than IFR navigation. Compared to IFR, the VFR pilot has more freedom to manoeuvre, but also has more responsibility to maintain situational awareness and safe separation from A/C and obstacles. Under VFR rules, pilots are their own clearance authority and are responsible for weather updates, traffic avoidance and separation, route planning, terrain avoidance, and airfield suitability. The goal of VFR navigation training is to get from one point to another by dead-reckoning (DR) techniques and procedures.

parameters.name: low-level introduction groundspeed
parameters.verbatim: While your initial introduction to low-level visual navigation will be flown at 210 KIAS groundspeed, the skills introduced in this course are essentially the same as those used in high performance A/C flying at 500 KIAS Indicated Airspeed (KIAS).

parameters.name: high performance A/C reference speed
parameters.verbatim: high performance A/C flying at 500 KIAS Indicated Airspeed (KIAS)

sections.notes: Your ability to properly prepare a navigation chart, study and interpret the information on the chart, and identify points on the ground while airborne determines the success of your mission.

sections.title: CHARTS (Navigational Charts, Scales, Chart Legend)
sections.technique_summary: The success of any mission depends on extensive crew pre-flight planning. The proper charts must be selected to cover the route of flight to the target, and the course to be flown must be plotted on the chart. The aircrew must be completely familiar with the symbols used on the chart so they can interpret them, navigate the A/C, and avoid all hazards during flight. A chart legend is the key explaining the meaning of the relief, culture, hydrography, vegetation, and aeronautical symbols.

parameters.name: long-range navigation charts
parameters.verbatim: Those applicable to long-range navigation methods, such as Operational Navigation Charts (ONC) 1:1,000,000 and IFR High Altitude Charts.

parameters.name: short-range navigation charts
parameters.value: TPC 1:500,000; IFR Low Altitude Charts; VFR Sectionals
parameters.verbatim: Those applicable to short-range navigation methods, such as Tactical Pilotage Charts (TPC) 1:500,000, IFR Low Altitude Charts, and VFR Sectionals.

parameters.name: 1:1.000.000 scale equivalence
parameters.verbatim: if the scale is 1:1.000.000, one inch of the chart represents 1.000.000 inches (about 14 miles) on the ground

parameters.name: 1:500,000 scale equivalence
parameters.verbatim: If the scale is 1:500,000, one inch of the chart represents 500,000 inches (about 7 miles) on the ground.

parameters.name: scale convention (large scale vs small scale)
parameters.value: 1:500,000 is larger than 1:1,000,000 — large scale = much detail, small area
parameters.verbatim: Note that a scale 1:500,000 is larger than 1:1,000,000 (a large scale chart gives you a large amount of detail and a small amount of area).

parameters.name: general planning scale
parameters.verbatim: The scale of charts used in general planning is 1:5.000.000 or 1:1.000.000.

parameters.name: detailed area planning scale
parameters.verbatim: For detailed area planning, a scale of 1:50.000 is generally used.

parameters.name: Navigation stage chart
parameters.verbatim: During the Navigation stage of instruction, the VFR Sectional aeronautical chart with a scale of 1:500.000 will be used.

parameters.name: two-lane road symbol exaggeration
parameters.value: about 20 times true scale (true width ≈ 0.0005 inch)
parameters.verbatim: The width of a two-lane road on the sectional is shown at about 20 times its true scale. If drafted exactly to half-millionth scale, the charted road would be only about 0.0005 inch wide.

parameters.name: lookout tower symbol size
parameters.value: about 1/2 nautical mile in diameter to scale
parameters.verbatim: The symbol for a lookout tower is about 1/2 nautical mile in diameter to scale on the sectional, even though its counterpart in the real world is much smaller.

parameters.name: VORTAC symbol size
parameters.value: almost a mile wide at sectional scale
parameters.verbatim: A VORTAC station is almost a mile wide as portrayed at sectional scale.

parameters.name: minor airport symbol size
parameters.verbatim: The open circle denoting a minor airport has a diameter of 4,000 feet to scale on the sectional, regardless of the actual size of the field.

procedure_steps: Select the proper charts to cover the route of flight to the target.

Choose the scale on the basis of the two governing factors: (1) the size of the area to be charted, as limited by the physical size of the chart; (2) the amount of detail to be shown, as limited by the probable use of the landmarks in navigation.
Plot the course to be flown on the chart.
Become completely familiar with every symbol contained on the chart by using the chart legend (Figure 8.3).
common_errors: The sizes of symbols do not always conform to true scale — judging real-world feature size from symbol size on the chart.

Selecting a detailed area planning chart (for example 1:50.000) whose coverage is too small for the mission: coverage that is too small for convenient use in fast A/C which rapidly “fly off” the chart necessitates frequent transfers to adjacent charts and the annoyance of having to fold and refold a large sheet in cramped quarters.
Failing to appreciate that discrepancies between the real world and its representation on an aeronautical chart are largely the results of limitations imposed by scale.
sections.notes: The location of one object relative to another (for example, a tower that is one mile north of a primary road) will have that distance accurately displayed on the chart, even where symbol sizes are exaggerated. Beware the cartographic convention when reading §8.15.2.c: a scale of 1:500,000 is LARGER than 1:1,000,000, so the detailed area planning chart (1:50.000) is a large-scale chart — what is “too small” about it is its coverage (area), not its scale.

sections.title: RELIEF (Contour Lines, Spot Elevations, MEF, Gradient Tints)
sections.technique_summary: Chart relief shows the physical features related to the differences in elevation of the earth's surface — mountains, hills, plateaus, plains, depressions, etc. Standard symbols and shading techniques are used in relief portrayal on charts; these include contours, spot elevations, variations in tint, and shading to represent shadows.

parameters.name: basic contour interval (Figure 8-4)
parameters.verbatim: In Figure 8-4, the basic contour interval is 1,000 feet.

parameters.name: MEF clearance added
parameters.verbatim: The MEF is determined by adding 100 to 199 feet of clearance over the highest known feature, including vertical obstructions (trees, towers, antennas).

parameters.name: MEF reading example
parameters.verbatim: Example: 125 means the highest feature within that grid is between 12,301 and 12,400 feet.

procedure_steps: Read contour lines: on steep slopes, the contour lines are close together and on gentle slopes, they are farther apart.
Identify depression contours — regular contour lines with spurs or ticks added on the down slope side.
Find the contour interval in the chart legend.
Use spot elevations — the heights of particular points of terrain above an established datum, usually mean sea level.
Use Maximum Elevation Figures (MEF), based on the highest point, natural or man-made, within a given grid square.
Use gradient (elevation) tints — the darker the tint the higher the elevation.
sections.notes: The interval of the contour lines usually depends upon the scale of the chart and the terrain depicted; intermediate and auxiliary contour intervals will vary depending on the scale of the chart.

sections.title: CULTURAL FEATURES (Roads, Bridges, Railroads, Power Lines, Populated Areas, Coastal Hydrography)
sections.technique_summary: All man-made structures appearing on the chart are known as cultural features. The amount of detail given to cultural features is governed by the scale of the chart, the use of the chart, and the geographical area covered. Transportation lines, consisting primarily of railroads and roads, are important features for use in obtaining time checks along your route; when used in conjunction with other features, they can help to determine A/C position.

parameters.name: bridge symbol threshold
parameters.verbatim: Bridges and viaducts over 500 feet long are portrayed with a bridge symbol in uncongested areas.

parameters.name: minimum bridge length of scale on sectional
parameters.verbatim: the minimum length of scale on the sectional is 2,000 feet between abutment ticks

parameters.name: double-line stream width
parameters.verbatim: bridge symbols will be shown where roads cross double-line streams (streams at least 600 feet wide)

parameters.name: power line crossing clearance
parameters.verbatim: Cross them 1000΄ feet higher and note the crossing altitude (MSL) on the map.

parameters.name: power line marking colour
parameters.verbatim: Consult the appropriate high-voltage grid map and mark them with red colour.

procedure_steps: Identify dual lane highways — indicated by a double line, the easiest type of transportation line to identify from the air.
Identify primary roads — portrayed as a single thick line; secondary roads — a single thin line; tracks and trails — a broken line.
Consult the high-voltage grid map, mark power transmission lines in red, cross them 1000΄ feet higher and note the crossing altitude (MSL) on the map.
Use populated areas as checkpoints, identified by some unique element which differentiates one city from another in the same area.

Distinguish the only two categories of populated areas shown on the chart: “a. Those of relatively large size and known shape, which are portrayed with city outlines. b. Those of a small size or unknown shape, which are shown by means of a small circle.”
Use coastlines for time checks inbound or outbound from the land, and for position determination if significant points or inlets are available.
common_errors: Counting roads as an orientation technique: “He should make no attempt to count roads as an orientation technique.”

Trusting the charted road classification: except for dual lane highways, the road classification shown on the chart may not be a reliable indication of the visual appearance of the road (particularly true of two-lane roads which may be encoded as primary or secondary).

Expecting all bridges to be charted — you can expect to see many bridges along the flight path that are not shown on the chart; their presence will have to be inferred by the fact that the road crosses a portrayed stream.
Judging bridge height from the symbol — the vertical development of bridges cannot be determined from the symbol; a tall bridge will appear the same on the chart as a low bridge.

Expecting railroads to be easy to see: railroads are not always easy to see from low altitude, even though they are portrayed boldly on the chart; they are easier to detect in hilly or mountainous terrain than in flat populated areas.
Relying on power transmission lines visually — they are generally difficult to see from the air.
Identifying a city from its charted outline alone: “you should not attempt to identify a city on this basis alone.” The city outline on the chart does not include recent suburban developments.
Being surprised by town size — do not be surprised if the town is much smaller or larger than you expected after looking at the chart; this holds especially true for small towns.
corrections: When positively identified, a bridge can be used to fix the A/C's position.
Identify roads that are seen but hard to classify on the basis of planned time of arrival.
Positively identify a city by a unique element which differentiates it from another city in the same area.
sections.notes: The portrayed built-up area is primarily intended to identify the location where the significant vertical development of the city exists.

sections.title: PRE-FLIGHT PLANNING — STEPS AND REFERENCE MATERIALS
sections.technique_summary: There are four important steps in pre-flight planning: acquiring navigational material and reference publications, route selection, chart preparation, and mission card preparation. Prior to any Navigation flight, it is imperative that the pilot thoroughly familiarize him/herself with intended routes of flight, possible alternate routes of flight, intended destination, possible alternates, and fuel requirements for each flight.

parameters.name: required documents
parameters.value: GR 1T-6A-11 FLIGHT MANUAL; ΜΑΙΡ (VOL I, II, SUPPLEMENT) - AIP GREECE; Local Area Procedures; In Flight Guide
parameters.verbatim: (1) GR 1T-6A-11 FLIGHT MANUAL (2) ΜΑΙΡ ( VOL I, II, SUPPLEMENT) - AIP GREECE (3) Local Area Procedures (4) In Flight Guide

procedure_steps: Acquire navigational material and reference publications.
Route selection.
Chart preparation.
Mission card preparation.
common_errors: Beginning the flight without thorough familiarization with intended routes, possible alternate routes, intended destination, possible alternates, and fuel requirements.

sections.title: ROUTE SELECTION
sections.technique_summary: There are two important steps to take prior to chart preparation: selection of a destination and selection of the route. Select a VFR destination within approximately 200-300 NM of the departure airport; this should allow for adequate fuel reserves to perform practice approaches and patterns at the destination. Routes should, at a minimum, have 6-8 checkpoints. Coordinate destination airport and route selection with your instructor prior to beginning your flight planning.

parameters.name: VFR destination distance
parameters.verbatim: As a rule of thumb, select a VFR destination within approximately 200-300 NM of the departure airport.

parameters.name: minimum checkpoints per route
parameters.verbatim: Routes should, at a minimum, have 6-8 checkpoints.

procedure_steps: Select the destination, then select the route; coordinate both with your instructor prior to beginning flight planning.
Obtain the route early so the proper pre-flight planning can be completed.
Once the destination is established, check the weather and acquire the terminal forecast at homefield and at the destination.
Obtain all available information pertaining to enroute weather, destination weather, and the forecast weather for the return flight.

Plan fuel including diverting to alternates along the entire route, minimum fuel along the route required to successfully divert (bingo), minimum fuel along the route to complete the mission as briefed, and emergency fuel requirements.
common_errors: Planning too few checkpoints — the more checkpoints along your route, the less chance you will get disoriented.
Fuel planning limited to a home field to destination computation, without accounting for diverts, bingo, mission completion and emergency fuel.
sections.notes: The choice of routes by the instructor is made with main consideration for the weather and a secondary consideration of distance, due to the fuel limitations of the T-6A.

sections.title: CHART PREPARATION — CHECKPOINTS, COURSE LINE, MAGNETIC COURSE, DISTANCE, TIMING TICS
sections.technique_summary: Select the charts to be used for the flight and check the dates of expiration to make certain they are current. Required equipment to lay out a route: dividers, navigational plotter, pencil, black ballpoint pen, highlighters and template for making circles, squares, and arrows. Each route segment should include route's legs, timing info, distance info, doghouses, North sign, ΜΤΜΑ, ΤΜΑ, CTR, ATZ, divertion lines, bird corridors, concentrations and other significant obstacles.

parameters.name: checkpoint circle diameter
parameters.verbatim: A circle diameter 1.6 cm should be drawn around each checkpoint for easy identification.

parameters.name: checkpoint spacing
parameters.value: no closer than 5 minutes and not more than 25 minutes apart
parameters.verbatim: As a rule, checkpoints should be no closer than 5 minutes and not more than 25 minutes apart.

parameters.name: T-6A turn radius
parameters.verbatim: Since the T-6A has a very small turn radius, it is considered as negligible. (60º bank /210 TAS 3.900’ turn radius → GR 1T-6A-11 σελ. A9-6).

parameters.name: magnetic course formula
parameters.value: TC – Variation (E) = MC; TC + Variation (W) = MC
parameters.verbatim: Compute magnetic course: TC – Variation (E) = MC TC + Variation (W) = MC

parameters.name: distance scale ticking
parameters.value: each 10 NM interval; last 10 NM block ticked at each 1 NM
parameters.verbatim: The scale should be ticked at each 10 NM interval. With the last 10 NM block being ticked at each 1 NM.

parameters.name: distance rounding
parameters.verbatim: Measure from center to center of each checkpoint and round off to the nearest one-half nautical mile.

parameters.name: planning groundspeed
parameters.verbatim: Figure timing between each leg based on 210 KIAS ground speed (3.5 miles/minute).

parameters.name: time tic marks
parameters.value: 1.2 cm every 2 minutes; 0,6 cm between each 2 minutes interval
parameters.verbatim: Place time tic marks (1.2 cm) perpendicular to the course line every 2 minutes as it is shown in Figure 8.7. Place 0,6 cm time tic marks between each 2 minutes interval.

parameters.name: distance plotting marks (Figure 8.7)
parameters.verbatim: Distance every 10 ΝΜ(0,6cm) and every 20 ΝΜ(1,2cm) number plotting.

parameters.name: airspace colour coding
parameters.value: TMA/MTMA blue; ATZ, CTR, Dangerous and Restricted Areas red; bird corridors green; bird concentration areas red
parameters.verbatim: TMA’s / MTMA’s: are highlighted in blue colour while ΑΤΖs, CTRs, Dangerous and Restricted Areas in red (name, vertical limits). Green colour is used for Bird corridors and red colour for Bird concentration areas.

procedure_steps: Select the charts and check the dates of expiration to make certain they are current.
Determine the end point or destination of your route — the final checkpoint is referred to as your target; the required time of arrival at this final checkpoint is your Time On Target (TOT).
Locate checkpoints along the route allowing you to navigate from the initial checkpoint to the final checkpoint; draw a 1.6 cm diameter circle around each.
Select prominent features on the chart that will be easily identified from the air; keep checkpoints no closer than 5 minutes and not more than 25 minutes apart.
Use the nav plotter to connect the points directly with a course line; stop the course line at the edge of the circle.
Use the longitude lines to get true heading; measure true course (TC) with the plotter, find the average isogonic variation for the route segment, and compute magnetic course.
Measure leg distances center to center of each checkpoint and round to the nearest one-half nautical mile; record on the Mission Card.
Figure leg timing based on 210 KIAS ground speed (3.5 miles/minute) and place the 1.2 cm / 0,6 cm time tic marks.
common_errors: Excessive chart marking: “As a general rule when preparing your chart is to minimize marking up the chart to avoid possibly obscuring potential needed information.”
Running the course line through the checkpoint circle: “Stop your course line at the edge of your circle to preclude obscuring important data over your checkpoint.”
Using an expired chart — check the dates of expiration to make certain they are current.
Selecting checkpoints that are not prominent features easily identified from the air.
corrections: Recommend all marks be done initially in pencil to allow easy correction. Ballpoint black ink can be used after all work is completed.
sections.notes: The interval between tic marks can be as restrictive as needed for the particular mission.

sections.title: CONTINUATION FUEL
sections.technique_summary: Continuation Fuel is the minimum amount of fuel required at each checkpoint to continue with the planned route and proceed to the final landing destination with required reserves. Compute Continuation Fuel by working backwards along your route of flight.

parameters.name: fuel reserves
parameters.verbatim: First, begin by adding fuel reserves (in accordance with local SOP) to the fuel required to transit from your landing destination to your final checkpoint.

procedure_steps: Begin by adding fuel reserves (in accordance with local SOP) to the fuel required to transit from the landing destination to the final checkpoint.
Add this amount to the fuel required to fly each leg of the flight plan from the final checkpoint back to the initial takeoff.
Note whether the final checkpoint is also the destination airport; if not, plan for the fuel to transit from the end of the route to the landing destination.
common_errors: Failing to note whether the final checkpoint is also the destination airport, so the transit fuel from route end to landing destination is not planned.
corrections: For primary navigation training, modifications or termination of the route early and proceeding direct to your final checkpoint are the expected courses of action if fuel to continue will be exceeded along the route.
sections.notes: Real world constraints may dictate a route/mission abort.

sections.title: TIME OVER TARGET (TOT) AND ROUTE TIMING
sections.technique_summary: Time Over Target (TOT) is the exact arrival time at the last checkpoint based upon the pre-planned total route time. Meeting a TOT can mean the difference of mission success or mission failure when working with other military assets. It is important to arrive at each checkpoint at the planned time so that arrival at the last checkpoint with correct TOT is attained. For timing corrections along the route, apply ground speed corrections based on the 60 to 1 rule.

parameters.name: start time (HACK)
parameters.value: 0+00 in the bottom of the first data box
parameters.verbatim: Begin by placing a start time (HACK) of 0+00 in the bottom of your first data box (first checkpoint).

parameters.name: planning groundspeed
parameters.value: 210 KIAS ground speed or 3.5 nautical miles per minute
parameters.verbatim: Let's look at a T-6A travelling at 210 KIAS ground speed or 3.5 nautical miles per minute.

parameters.name: timing correction basis
parameters.verbatim: Timing corrections are based on the 60 to 1 rule.

parameters.name: timing correction rule (60 to 1)
parameters.value: for every ten seconds off timing, change the ground speed by 10 KIAS for 3,5 minutes
parameters.verbatim: For every ten seconds off timing, change the ground speed by 10 KIAS for 3,5 minutes.

parameters.name: timing correction example
parameters.value: 40 seconds ahead → decrease ground speed to 170 KIAS for 3,5 minutes
parameters.verbatim: For example: If you are 40 seconds ahead, decrease the ground speed to 170 KIAS for 3,5 minutes.

procedure_steps: Place a start time (HACK) of 0+00 in the bottom of the first data box (first checkpoint).
Calculate the time enroute for the first leg and enter it into the second data box for elapsed time.
On subsequent legs continue adding leg time to the previous elapsed time.
Verify that elapsed time at the final checkpoint (TOT) equals the total pre-planned time enroute.
Sequentially number each checkpoint on the route to the right of the checkpoint.
By noting the clock at the time of route commencement, determine a hard time (actual arrival time) for each checkpoint in advance.
common_errors: Cutting off or extending the route to fix timing: “For timing corrections along the route, cutting off or extending your route is not the best course of action.”
corrections: A better method is to apply ground speed corrections, based on the 60 to 1 rule.
When back on time, analyze why you got off time and apply corrections to your ground speed.

sections.title: DATA BOX
sections.technique_summary: Draw a data box along each route segment, pointing in the direction that the leg is to be flown. A data box may contain as much or as little information as necessary. For the Primary Navigation stage, fill in the information as shown in Figure 8-8.

parameters.name: turn point number
parameters.value: same as in navigation card, starting from number 2
parameters.verbatim: Turn Point Number: Should be the same as in navigation card, starting from number 2.

parameters.name: leg length
parameters.value: integer number approximated to the nearest
parameters.verbatim: Leg Length: Integer number approximated to the nearest.

parameters.name: leg time
parameters.verbatim: Leg Time: In minutes and seconds

parameters.name: min safe altitude (per leg)
parameters.value: highest top's altitude inside the 5NM buffer zone approximated to the nearest hundred +500'
parameters.verbatim: Min Safe Altitude (for each leg): This derives from the highest top’s altitude inside the 5NM buffer zone approximated to the nearest hundred +500’.

parameters.name: continuation fuel
parameters.value: fuel required at the beginning of each leg to complete the rest of the navigation and reach the BREAK with NORMAL RECOVERY
parameters.verbatim: Continuation Fuel: Is the amount of fuel that I should have at the beginning of each leg in order to complete the rest of the navigation and reach the BREAK with NORMAL RECOVERY. For this reason, this fuel has to be calculated starting from the last point of the navigation.

procedure_steps: Draw a data box along each route segment, pointing in the direction that the leg is to be flown.
Fill in: (1) Turn Point Number, (2) Leg Magnetic Heading (corrected per chart legend), (3) Leg Length, (4) Leg Time, (5) Min Safe Altitude, (6) Continuation Fuel.
common_errors: Placing the data box over usable terrain: “Do not obscure any geographical features usable for navigation.”

sections.title: LANDMARKS (Positive, Linear, Uncertain)
sections.technique_summary: Study the route and note landmarks that can be used as a time check or as a position check. There are three types of landmarks: positive landmarks, which can be positively identified and plotted at a point on the chart; linear landmarks, which can be positively identified but not specifically plotted because they extend for some distance; and uncertain landmarks, which the pilot suspects he/she can correlate with the chart but are not fully reliable.
procedure_steps: Study the route and note landmarks usable as a time check or a position check.

Classify landmarks as positive (e.g. a large distinctively shaped lake, an airport, or a road with a prominent bend), linear (rivers, roads, railroad tracks), or uncertain (small lakes, farms, oil fields, or towers).
common_errors: Basing a heading correction on an uncertain landmark: uncertain landmarks “may not be used as the basis for a heading correction.”
corrections: Uncertain landmarks indicate to the pilot a likely position from which he/she can better anticipate future landmarks.

sections.title: NAVIGATION CARD
sections.technique_summary: The Navigation Card includes turning points, coordinates, magnetic headings, leg distances, remaining distance, leg time, total time, leg fuel, remaining fuel, safety altitudes, total distance, BINGO point, and Route Abort altitude.

parameters.name: navigation card contents
parameters.value: turning points, coordinates, magnetic headings, leg distances, remaining distance, leg time, total time, leg fuel, remaining fuel, safety altitudes, total distance, BINGO point, Route Abort altitude
parameters.verbatim: Navigation Card. Includes turning points, coordinates, magnetic headings, leg distances, remaining distance, leg time, total time, leg fuel, remaining fuel, safety altitudes, total distance, BINGO point, Route Abort altitude.

sections.title: AIRSPACE ANNOTATION AND EMERGENCY AIRFIELDS (DIVERSION LINES)
sections.technique_summary: Annotate MTMA's, TMA's, LGD's, LGR's, bird corridors, concentration areas and emergency airfields (divertion lines). During flight planning, suitable airfields must be selected along the planned flight route as possible emergency landing areas, drawing diversion lines of 10 nm length.

parameters.name: diversion line length
parameters.verbatim: suitable airfields must be selected along the planned flight route as possible emergency landing areas drawing diversion lines 10 nm length

procedure_steps: Annotate MTMA's, TMA's, LGD's, LGR's, bird corridors, concentration areas and emergency airfields (divertion lines).

Select emergency airfields along the route: mentally join the two suitable closest emergency airports and mentally draw the line bisector; the point where the route is intersected defines the new Emergency Airfield which must be chosen in case of an abnormal situation.
Draw diversion lines 10 nm in length.
sections.notes: Emergency airfields are depicted in red colour (Figure 8-11).

sections.title: NAVIGATION PROCEDURES — INTRODUCTION
sections.technique_summary: The key to any successful flight can be directly attributed to sound procedures. Much like the Instrument Stage, a good scan, thorough pre-flight planning, and the 6 Ts, will equip any aviator with the tools necessary for successful navigation.

sections.title: COCKPIT MANAGEMENT (CRM / student responsibilities)
sections.technique_summary: Before each flight, Crew Resource Management (CRM) will be discussed during the Pre Flight briefing. It should cover the conduct of the flight and what is expected from both the instructor pilot and student. In the training environment, the student will normally be the pilot at the controls.

parameters.name: operations checks interval
parameters.verbatim: Perform Operations checks every 15-20 minutes and update closest divert field.

procedure_steps: a. Navigation and mission requirements.
b. Radio calls.
c. Timing between checkpoints and continuous update of course and airspeed corrections as well as time on target (TOT) updates if required.
d. Landmark identification.
e. Management of all radio frequencies.
f. Perform Operations checks every 15-20 minutes and update closest divert field.

sections.title: GROUND PROCEDURES (VFR Navigation)
sections.technique_summary: All checklists shall be accomplished to the Flight Manual. Before leaving the holding position area, ensure your charts, logs and pubs are open and readily accessible for the flight. Be organized.
procedure_steps: Accomplish all checklists to the Flight Manual.
Before leaving the holding position area, ensure charts, logs and pubs are open and readily accessible for the flight.
common_errors: Leaving chart and card organization until after takeoff: “The departure climb out is not the time to have to fold your chart or look for your Mission Card.”

sections.title: DEPARTURE (VFR Navigation)
sections.technique_summary: Takeoff and departure will be in accordance with LAP. Level off at altitude using normal procedures. Stabilize on heading and altitude to the first checkpoint if possible. Trim! Cruise control procedures are very important to a successful flight. Good trim ensures accurate altitude and heading control, even fuel flow, and will minimize pilot fatigue.
procedure_steps: Take off and depart in accordance with LAP.
Level off at altitude using normal procedures.
Stabilize on heading and altitude to the first checkpoint if possible.
Trim.
Maintain a continuous VFR scan of the surrounding airspace and engine instruments to ensure flight safety.
common_errors: Poor trim, which degrades accurate altitude and heading control and even fuel flow, and increases pilot fatigue.

sections.title: ROUTE ENTRY
sections.technique_summary: The first few minutes of a VFR leg can be very challenging. Many tasks must be performed including getting established on the desired route at the appropriate altitude and airspeed. Maneuver the A/C to hit the entry point on the first leg heading and airspeed. Proper planning and a solid review of the planned departure ground track make route entry tasks more manageable.
procedure_steps: Before the entry point, accomplish a descent check.
Prepare the clock and review the time hack procedure with the other pilot.
Identify the entry point as early as possible.
Maneuver the A/C to hit the entry point on the first leg heading and airspeed.
Make the appropriate route entry call.
common_errors: Identifying the entry point late, so the A/C cannot be maneuvered to hit the entry point on the first leg heading and airspeed.

sections.title: NAVIGATION — DEAD RECKONING, PILOTAGE AND TASK MANAGEMENT
sections.technique_summary: The primary means of navigation used on Navigation flights will be a combination of dead reckoning (DR) and pilotage. DR is a logical system in which time, velocity, and distance are combined to arrive at a position. Pilotage is flying by visual reference to features on the ground. Task management may be divided into two basic components: terrain clearance tasks (TCT), avoiding the ground, and mission tasks (MT), accomplishing the mission.
procedure_steps: Combine dead reckoning (time, velocity, distance) with pilotage (visual reference to features on the ground).

Terrain Clearance Tasks — avoiding the ground is the number one priority; clear and maneuver the A/C, avoid the ground and objects attached to the ground, primarily by looking outside the cockpit to see and avoid.
Mission Tasks — in flight checks, fuel calculations, timing and route corrections.
common_errors: Performing mission tasks for an extended time: “Never perform MTs for an extended time.”
Allowing mission tasks to degrade terrain clearance.
corrections: If mission tasks degrade terrain clearance, CLIMB!
sections.notes: The amount of time spent between TCTs and MTs depends on several factors such as altitude, airspeed, weather, and crew capability.

sections.title: ROUTE BASICS — MISSION ELEMENT PRIORITIES
sections.technique_summary: Sound task prioritization and an organized approach are essential to a successful mission. On the route, distinct mission elements must be integrated, in priority order: Safety, Systems Operation, Navigation, Priority (clearing), Trim the A/C, Clock-Map-Ground, Identify, and Checkpoint Procedures.

parameters.name: turns share of flying vs mishaps
parameters.value: turns make up 10 % of flying in the low level environment; they account for over 50 % of the mishaps
parameters.verbatim: While turns make up 10 % of flying in the low level environment, they account for over 50 % of the mishaps.

parameters.name: clearing time allocation
parameters.value: eighty % heads up and eyes out
parameters.verbatim: Clearing is the highest priority task; eighty % of your time flying low level should be spent “heads up and eyes out.”

parameters.name: cruise power for planned groundspeed
parameters.verbatim: Trim the A/C and set the proper IAS or power setting for the planned groundspeed, approximately 65% torque for 210 KIAS.

procedure_steps: (1) Safety — stay clear of terrain, obstacles, and other A/C. Focus on terrain clearance is especially critical during turns.
(2) Systems Operation — perform required checks; monitor systems and fuel consumption.
(3) Navigation — follow route and identify required points; meet timing goal.
(4) Priority — clearing is the highest priority task; always return the focus to clearing outside; bring the chart up to eye level to read it.
(5) Trim the A/C and set the proper IAS or power setting for the planned groundspeed, approximately 65% torque for 210 KIAS.
common_errors: Insufficient focus on terrain clearance during turns — turns make up 10 % of flying in the low level environment but account for over 50 % of the mishaps.
Spending less than eighty % of low-level time “heads up and eyes out.”
Reading the chart down in the cockpit instead of bringing it up to eye level.
corrections: Always return the focus to clearing outside.
Bring the chart up to eye level to read it.

sections.title: CLOCK-MAP-GROUND METHOD
sections.technique_summary: Use the Clock-Map-Ground method when reading your chart: check timing and find the corresponding location on the chart, then look outside to find the feature that matches the chart. This method will prove to be remarkably accurate when combined with careful heading control. A recommended method is to align the chart in the same relative direction as the A/C's actual track.

parameters.name: attention focus distance
parameters.value: points that are 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead of the A/C
parameters.verbatim: Focus attention on points that are 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead of the A/C.

parameters.name: checkpoint look-ahead
parameters.value: 2-5 minutes ahead, identified by 1 minute out
parameters.verbatim: Look for checkpoints 2-5 minutes ahead and have them identified by 1 minute out.

parameters.name: prominent points per leg
parameters.verbatim: Look for at least one or two prominent points on each leg.

procedure_steps: Check timing and find the corresponding location on the chart.
Look outside to find the feature that matches the chart.
Look for at least one or two prominent points on each leg; focus attention on points 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead.
Check the chart for preselected checkpoints, then look ahead on the ground for the point identified by the chart.
Look for checkpoints 2-5 minutes ahead and have them identified by 1 minute out; crosscheck against timing.
Use cockpit reference points in order to determine exact outside points according to your A/C.
Align the chart in the same relative direction as the A/C's actual track.
common_errors: Reversing the method (ground-to-map) instead of chart-to-ground: the correct procedure is to check the chart for preselected checkpoints, then look ahead on the ground for the point identified by the chart.
Crosschecking navigation with only references off the nose of the A/C: “Do not limit yourself to crosschecking your navigation with only references off the nose of the A/C.”
Failing to note the relationship of how landmarks are arranged in relation to one another.
corrections: Exercise a scan to include as far as you can see in each direction to assist with your navigation.

Use the relationship between landmarks to disambiguate: for example, if two small towns lie ahead and you are unsure which one is your next checkpoint, the existence of several towers to the east of one city may help to identify the correct checkpoint.

sections.title: IDENTIFY TURN POINTS AND CHECKPOINT PROCEDURES (6 Ts)
sections.technique_summary: Start trying to identify turn points about one to one and a half minutes out. If possible, verify the point with multiple features. If the point is not identified, turn on time. Turns at low altitude require extra emphasis on clearing and A/C control. Once positive identification of a checkpoint has been made, fly directly over the checkpoint and perform the 6 Ts: Time, Turn, Throttle, Twist, Track, Talk.

parameters.name: turn point identification lead time
parameters.value: about one to one and a half minutes out
parameters.verbatim: Start trying to identify turn points about one to one and a half minutes out.

parameters.name: altitude threshold — incomplete sentence in source
parameters.value: below 3000 feet AGL (the manual does not state what must be ensured)
parameters.verbatim: If operating below 3000 feet AGL, ensure.

procedure_steps: Start trying to identify turn points about one to one and a half minutes out; if possible, verify the point with multiple features.
Clear in the direction of the turn; select a visual rollout reference, turn to the visual reference, then fine tune heading.
Fly directly over the checkpoint once positively identified and perform the 6 Ts:
(a) Time – Note the time at the checkpoint; this time should correspond with your leg time and elapsed time.
(b) Turn – Turn to the new heading and look for a landmark off the nose to aid in heading control.
(c) Throttle – Adjust torque according to new airspeed.
(d) Twist – Heading bug on appropriate heading.
(e) Track – course centerline at desired altitude.

(f) Talk – to the appropriate frequency; check that the altitude is in conformance with VFR cruising procedures; climb or descend as necessary using normal procedures prior to the checkpoint to be at the appropriate altitude before commencing the next leg.
common_errors: Delaying a turn because the point is not identified: “If the point is not identified, turn on time.”
Reduced clearing and A/C control during low-altitude turns — turns at low altitude require extra emphasis on clearing and A/C control.
corrections: If the point is not identified, turn on time.
Clearing is enhanced by selection of a visual rollout reference; turn to the visual reference, then fine tune heading.
Climb or descend as necessary using normal procedures prior to the checkpoint to be at the appropriate altitude before commencing the next leg.
sections.notes: The manual text is defective at the end of §(f) Talk (page 191): the sentence «If operating below 3000 feet AGL, ensure.» is truncated in the source and never states what must be ensured. No requirement is to be inferred from it.

sections.title: BIG PICTURE AND ALTITUDE CONTROL
sections.technique_summary: Keep an eye on the big picture. Use major terrain features (mountains, lakes, obvious geological formations, etc.) to improve positional awareness. Visually assess the height above the ground and occasionally crosscheck the altimeter against the known elevation of towers, lakes, airfields, and peak elevations. Visual navigation is easier as altitude increases; climb early if in doubt and the route structure allows it.

parameters.name: Time to Impact (TTI) chart
parameters.verbatim: Figure is a Time to Impact (TTI) chart at 240 KIAS.

procedure_steps: Use major terrain features (mountains, lakes, obvious geological formations, etc.) to improve positional awareness.
Visually assess the height above the ground; occasionally crosscheck the altimeter against the known elevation of towers, lakes, airfields, and peak elevations.
Climb early if in doubt and the route structure allows it.
During turns, fly the A/C and clear; do nothing else.
common_errors: Performing other tasks during turns instead of flying the A/C and clearing: “During turns, fly the A/C and clear; do nothing else.”
corrections: Visual navigation is easier as altitude increases; climb early if in doubt and the route structure allows it.
sections.notes: Figure 8-12 is a Time to Impact (TTI) chart at 240 KIAS.

sections.title: WEATHER DEVIATIONS (Deliberate Course Duration Method)
sections.technique_summary: Occasionally you may encounter serious weather across your proposed route. It may be necessary to return to home field, go to an alternate destination, or possibly deviate from the planned route and circumnavigate the weather. If circumnavigation is possible, the deliberate course duration method should be used.

parameters.name: outbound heading change
parameters.verbatim: Leave the route by making a turn a number of degrees (i.e., 60º), determined by the distance and size of the obstructing weather.

parameters.name: return turn
parameters.verbatim: Note the time again and turn back toward the original course using twice the original heading change.

parameters.name: maximum recommended angle
parameters.verbatim: It is recommended that no angle above 70º be used.

parameters.name: inbound leg timing
parameters.value: same as outbound leg (assuming crosswinds negligent)
parameters.verbatim: The amount of time on the inbound leg will be the same as that for the outbound leg, (assuming crosswinds to be negligent).

parameters.name: ETA update with 60º method
parameters.value: add the leg time of one leg to the ETA
parameters.verbatim: If 60º heading changes are used, it is possible to update the ETA to the next checkpoints by adding the leg time of one leg to the ETA.

procedure_steps: Leave the route by making a turn a number of degrees (i.e., 60º), determined by the distance and size of the obstructing weather.
Note the time and maintain the new heading until abeam the obstruction.
Note the time again and turn back toward the original course using twice the original heading change.
Record the heading change and the time of the deviation on your kneeboard.
Fix the flight's position abeam the storm to determine outbound leg time; total outbound time is from turn outbound to turn inbound.
Fly the inbound leg for the same amount of time as the outbound leg; turn to the original heading at completion of timing on the inbound leg.
common_errors: Using a deviation angle above 70º — “It is recommended that no angle above 70º be used.”
Failing to record the heading change and the time of the deviation on the kneeboard.
sections.notes: The amount of heading change is determined by how extensive the storm is and how close your track is to the weather.

sections.title: STANDARD COURSE CORRECTIONS (SCA) AND WINGTIP REFERENCES
sections.technique_summary: Prior to takeoff, estimate your course and ground speed from known data. Once in the air, be prepared to adjust your heading for winds; crabbing into the wind may be necessary in order to stay on the planned course. Precise heading control is a must. Approaching a major checkpoint, positively identify it; if off track, determine approximately how far off course in ½ mile increments and correct using the Standard Closing Angle (SCA).

parameters.name: off-course estimation increment
parameters.verbatim: If off track, determine approximately how far off course in ½ mile increments.

parameters.name: wingtip reference at 1000 feet AGL
parameters.verbatim: At 1000 feet AGL, one wingtip is approximately 1NM (1500 ft = 1.5NM / 2000 ft = 2.0NM / 2500 ft = 2.5 NM).

parameters.name: wingtip geometry
parameters.value: 3 feet vertical height to 17 feet length to the wingtip = 1-5 ratio
parameters.verbatim: 3 feet vertical height compared to an 17 feet length to the wingtip gives a 1-5 ratio . That ratio is carried all the way down the line of sight giving approximate distances to objects on the ground.

parameters.name: T-6A wingtip distances
parameters.verbatim: For the T-6A, one wingtip distance is approximately equal to: 1500ft AGL = 1,5nm 2000ft AGL = 2,0nm 2500ft AGL = 2,5nm

parameters.name: SCA formula
parameters.verbatim: The SCA is based on the 60-1 rule and is calculated by taking 60 divided by your GS in NM/min.

parameters.name: SCA at 210 KGS
parameters.verbatim: For 210 KGS, the SCA is 17,5 degrees.

parameters.name: SCA hold time
parameters.value: 1 minute for every mile off course
parameters.verbatim: This means that you would make a 17,5 degree course correction from your planned heading and hold this correction for 1 minute for every mile off course. Every mile off course is equal to the number of minutes you hold to get back on course.

procedure_steps: Prior to takeoff, estimate course and ground speed from known data.
Adjust heading for winds; crab into the wind as necessary to stay on the planned course.
Set the heading bug on the wind corrected heading; set the CDI on the next leg's course.
Approaching a major checkpoint, positively identify it.
If off track, estimate distance off course in ½ mile increments (one method is wingtip references).
Apply the SCA: 60 divided by GS in NM/min (17,5 degrees for 210 KGS), held for 1 minute per mile off course.
Once back on course, analyze why you got off course and adjust heading appropriately.
common_errors: Imprecise heading control — “Precise heading control is a must.”
Failing to anticipate that a strong headwind or tailwind would cause differences in your timing.
corrections: Another correction method is funneling, which follows some linear landmark until it intercepts a positive landmark along or on your route of flight.

Use limiting features — prominent landmarks selected along your route of flight that prevent you from flying off course or beyond your checkpoint (if you are unable to locate the checkpoint and you subsequently find the chosen landmark, you know you have passed the checkpoint).

sections.title: STANDARD TIMING CORRECTIONS (Proportional Method)
sections.technique_summary: To correct for timing errors along the level route, use the proportional method: for every second off your planned ETA, change your IAS by 1 knot and hold this new airspeed for the number of minutes equal to your GS in NM/min. Fractions and multiples of this method may be used to adjust speeds and timing.

parameters.name: reference groundspeed
parameters.verbatim: We will use 210 KIAS ground speed in the examples below

parameters.name: proportional method rule
parameters.value: 1 knot per second off ETA, held for minutes equal to GS in NM/min
parameters.verbatim: Using the proportional method, for every second off your planned ETA, change your IAS by 1 knot and hold this new airspeed for the number of minutes equal to your GS in NM/min.

parameters.name: example correction
parameters.verbatim: If you are 20 seconds late, increase airspeed by 20 KIAS and hold this correction for 3+30 minutes.

parameters.name: equivalent corrections
parameters.value: 10 KIAS for 7+00 minutes or 40 KIAS for 1+45 minutes
parameters.verbatim: Instead of 20 KIAS for 3+30 minutes, you could use either 10 KIAS for 7+00 minutes or 40 KIAS for 1+45 minutes.

procedure_steps: Determine seconds off planned ETA.
Change IAS by 1 knot per second off ETA.
Hold the new airspeed for the number of minutes equal to your GS in NM/min.
Use fractions and multiples of this method as required.
common_errors: Holding the course for a checkpoint that cannot be recognized: “If the estimated time for a leg is up and you cannot recognize the checkpoint, turn on time to your next course, perform the checkpoint procedures, and look for landmarks that will enable you to identify your position.”
corrections: Once an accurate fix on your position has been determined, correct as necessary and revise your log.

sections.title: ABNORMAL PROCEDURES — EMERGENCIES (CLIMB TO COPE)
sections.technique_summary: The first reaction to any emergency encountered at low level is to climb. This action is referred as “climb to cope.” Climb as high as necessary to safely analyze the situation.
procedure_steps: Climb — “climb to cope.”
Climb as high as necessary to safely analyze the situation.

sections.title: ENGINE MALFUNCTIONS AT LOW LEVEL
sections.technique_summary: If the engine fails on a low-level route, recovery is unlikely unless a suitable landing field is within approximately 3 miles. As a technique, airfields within an arc circumscribed by the wingtips can be reached with an immediate turn and climb in the direction of the airfield. Map study for potential emergency diverts before the mission will greatly enhance chances for success.

parameters.name: recovery range
parameters.verbatim: If the engine fails on a low-level route, recovery is unlikely unless a suitable landing field is within approximately 3 miles.

parameters.name: zoom altitude gain
parameters.value: a zoom from 210 KGS gains approximately 1000 feet
parameters.verbatim: A zoom from 210 KGS gains approximately 1000 feet.

parameters.name: ejection decision
parameters.value: no N1 rise by the apex of the zoom → eject
parameters.verbatim: If there are no indications of a start (N1 rise) by the apex of the zoom, eject.

parameters.name: air start altitude limit
parameters.verbatim: Do not delay ejection to attempt air starts below 2000 AGL or if no airfields are within engine-out range.

procedure_steps: Make an immediate turn and climb in the direction of a suitable airfield within the arc circumscribed by the wingtips.
Consider a restart in the zoom.
If there are no indications of a start (N1 rise) by the apex of the zoom, eject.
common_errors: Delaying ejection to attempt air starts below 2000 AGL or when no airfields are within engine-out range.
Omitting map study for potential emergency diverts before the mission.

sections.title: MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE (MSA), EMERGENCY ROUTE ABORT ALTITUDE (ERAA) AND ROUTE ABORTS
sections.technique_summary: All Navigation routes will include a Minimum Safe Altitude (MSA) for each leg of the planned route. Aircrew experiencing temporary disorientation with regard to navigation will climb to MSA until positive position is regained. The higher MSA of the legs of the planned route will be the Emergency Route Abort Altitude (ERAA). Route aborts occur for various reasons: insufficient fuel to complete the route, A/C malfunction, bird hazards, and weather.

parameters.name: MSA definition
parameters.value: 500' higher than the highest obstacle (rounded up to the nearest 100' interval) within 5 NM of route centerline and 5 NM perimetrical of the two turnpoints
parameters.verbatim: The MSA will be 500’ higher than the highest obstacle (rounded up to the nearest 100’ interval) within 5 NM of route centerline as well as 5 NM perimetrical of the two turnpoints.

parameters.name: ERAA definition
parameters.value: the higher MSA of the legs of the planned route
parameters.verbatim: An Emergency Route Abort Altitude (ERAA). The higher MSA of the legs of the planned route will be the Emergency Route Abort Altitude.

parameters.name: IMC abort squawk
parameters.verbatim: Execute an immediate climb to the emergency route abort altitude (minimum) and squawk 7700.

procedure_steps: Aircrew experiencing temporary disorientation with regard to navigation will climb to MSA until positive position is regained.
Use the map, GPS, and NAVAIDs to maintain positional awareness or to find the nearest suitable recovery airfield.

VMC abort — maintain safe separation from the terrain, comply with VFR altitude restrictions (if possible), squawk an appropriate transponder code, maintain VMC, and attempt contact with a controlling agency, if required.

IMC abort — execute an immediate climb to the emergency route abort altitude (minimum), squawk 7700, attempt contact with the appropriate ATC agency, and fly the proper VFR altitude until an IFR clearance is received.
common_errors: Low-altitude flight increases the danger of distraction and complicates recovery.
corrections: An abort into IMC is an emergency — climb immediately to the ERAA (minimum) and squawk 7700.

sections.title: LOST A/C (Temporary Disorientation)
sections.technique_summary: A cool head is the pilot's best asset should he/she become temporarily disoriented. Determine the extent of disorientation, check the clock immediately, do not complicate the situation, and check fuel state against the minimum fuel required to continue to complete the route.

parameters.name: Five Cs
parameters.value: confess, climb, communicate, conserve, and comply
parameters.verbatim: remember the “Five Cs” (confess, climb, communicate, conserve, and comply) before your fuel state becomes a significant factor

procedure_steps: a. Determine the extent of disorientation; review progress from the last known position and determine the cause and extent of error.
b. Check the clock immediately and write down the time.

c. Do not complicate the situation; immediately upon realizing a problem exists, decide on a temporary plan — normally, continue flying pre-planned headings and times or fly toward a charted known landmark.
d. Check fuel state against the Minimum Fuel Required to continue to complete the route; remember the “Five Cs”.
common_errors: “Anxiety disorientation” — can occur even with the pilot exactly on course if his/her “chart-to-ground” method fails to identify an anticipated landmark and he/she misconstrues it as proof of being lost.
Wandering aimlessly while planning what to do next: “Avoid wandering aimlessly while planning what to do next.”
corrections: Causes of disorientation to review include: pilot errors in heading and airspeed control, timing, navigation chart planning; malfunction of instruments or navigation aids; wind; or deviations around weather or enemy defences.
sections.notes: Timing may be a factor in determining the extent of disorientation and required correction.
